courses.title: 1. Kernel space and your first module
courses.summary: Kernel space vs user space, loadable kernel modules, and building/loading a hello-world module with insmod, rmmod and dmesg.
courses.expected: After `make` and `sudo insmod hello.ko`, `sudo dmesg` shows 'hello: module loaded'; `sudo rmmod hello` logs 'hello: module unloaded'.

lessons.title: Kernel space vs user space
paragraphs: The CPU runs code in two privilege levels. User space (applications) is isolated: a crash kills one process. Kernel space runs with full hardware access in a single shared address space, so a kernel bug can corrupt memory or hang the whole machine.

User programs ask the kernel for privileged work through system calls. Kernel code never calls libc, has a small fixed stack, and must not use floating point — it is a different world from ordinary C programming.
lessons.example: A null-pointer bug in user space segfaults one process; in the kernel it can panic the box.
lessons.pitfall: Writing kernel code as if it were a normal C program (libc calls, big stack buffers, floats) does not even compile, or crashes the machine.

question.prompt: A bug in kernel space can:

options.text: corrupt memory or hang the whole system

question.explanation: The kernel has no isolation from itself.

lessons.title: Loadable kernel modules
paragraphs: A loadable kernel module (LKM) is kernel code you can insert and remove at runtime without rebooting, the usual way device drivers and filesystems are delivered. It is compiled to a .ko file against the running kernel's headers.
A module registers an init function (run on load) and an exit function (run on unload). `insmod` loads it, `rmmod` removes it, `lsmod` lists loaded modules, and `modinfo` shows its metadata.
lessons.example:
# Makefile (the recipe lines MUST start with a real tab, not spaces):
obj-m += hello.o
KDIR ?= /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build
all:
	$(MAKE) -C $(KDIR) M=$(PWD) modules
clean:
	$(MAKE) -C $(KDIR) M=$(PWD) clean
lessons.pitfall: Building a module against headers that do not match `uname -r` produces a .ko that insmod refuses with version-magic errors.

question.prompt: A loadable kernel module lets you add kernel code:
question.explanation: insmod/rmmod load and unload at runtime.

lessons.title: printk, log levels and dmesg
paragraphs: The kernel cannot printf to a terminal; it logs with printk and its helpers (pr_info, pr_err, pr_warn), each carrying a log level. Messages go to the kernel ring buffer, read with `dmesg`.
pr_info uses the KERN_INFO level; pr_err uses KERN_ERR. Log levels decide what reaches the console versus only the buffer, so use the right severity.
lessons.example: pr_info("x=%d\n", x);  // read it back with: dmesg | tail
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting the trailing \n in a printk makes the next message concatenate onto the same line in the log.

question.prompt: Kernel messages are read with:
question.explanation: printk writes the ring buffer; dmesg reads it.

lessons.title: Licensing and module metadata
paragraphs: Every module must declare MODULE_LICENSE. A non-GPL declaration taints the kernel and hides GPL-only symbols from the module. MODULE_AUTHOR and MODULE_DESCRIPTION are metadata shown by modinfo; recent toolchains warn if the description is missing.
The init function returns 0 on success or a negative errno (like -ENOMEM) on failure, which aborts the load. Clean error handling in init is essential because a half-initialized module is dangerous.
lessons.example: MODULE_LICENSE("GPL"); MODULE_DESCRIPTION("..."); // metadata for modinfo
lessons.pitfall: Omitting MODULE_LICENSE taints the kernel and can block access to many kernel symbols your module needs.

question.prompt: An init function signals failure by returning:

steps: Save the source as hello.c, and create a Makefile next to it from the 'Loadable kernel modules' lesson above (its recipe lines must begin with a real tab). Build other courses by changing obj-m to that lesson's file. Then run make.
Run `make`, then `sudo insmod hello.ko`, and check `sudo dmesg | tail` for the load message.
Run `sudo rmmod hello` and confirm the unload message; inspect metadata with `modinfo hello.ko`.
Explain why a kernel oops is more dangerous than a user-space segfault.

courses.title: 2. Module parameters and the build system
courses.summary: Pass parameters into a module, understand the out-of-tree Kbuild build, and see how exported symbols and tainting work.
courses.expected: `sudo insmod params.ko count=3 who=kernel` logs three greetings to 'kernel'; the values appear under /sys/module/params/parameters/.

lessons.title: Module parameters
paragraphs: module_param(name, type, perm) exposes a variable as a parameter that can be set at load time (insmod name=value) and, with non-zero permissions, read or written through /sys/module/<name>/parameters/.
Supported types include int, charp (string), bool and arrays. MODULE_PARM_DESC documents each one for modinfo. Parameters are how you configure a driver without recompiling it.
lessons.example: module_param(count, int, 0444); // set with: insmod mod.ko count=3
lessons.pitfall: Giving a parameter writable sysfs permissions (0644) without handling concurrent changes can race with the code that reads it.

question.prompt: module_param exposes a variable that can be set:

options.text: at insmod time and via sysfs

lessons.title: The Kbuild out-of-tree build
paragraphs: Modules are built with the kernel's own build system, Kbuild. An out-of-tree module uses a tiny Makefile: `obj-m += name.o` tells Kbuild what to build, and you invoke the kernel build directory with `make -C /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules`.

This compiles against the exact configuration and headers of the target kernel, producing a .ko with matching version magic. The kernel-headers (or kernel-devel) package provides that build directory.
lessons.example: obj-m += mymod.o   # then: make -C /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules
lessons.pitfall: Compiling a module with plain `gcc file.c` instead of Kbuild produces an object that is not a loadable module and lacks version magic.

question.prompt: obj-m += foo.o in a Makefile tells Kbuild to build:

lessons.title: Exported symbols
paragraphs: The kernel and modules share functions through exported symbols. A symbol is only visible to modules if it is exported with EXPORT_SYMBOL or EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL; the GPL variant is visible only to GPL-licensed modules.
This is why MODULE_LICENSE matters for linking: a proprietary module cannot see EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL symbols. `cat /proc/kallsyms` lists kernel symbols and their addresses.
lessons.example: EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL(my_func);  // visible only to GPL modules
lessons.pitfall: Calling a kernel function that is not exported fails at module load with an 'unknown symbol' error, not at compile time.

question.prompt: EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL makes a symbol visible to:

lessons.title: Tainting the kernel
paragraphs: The kernel tracks a 'taint' state recording conditions that make bug reports less trustworthy: a proprietary module loaded, a module force-loaded, a previous oops, and more. `dmesg` shows taint flags and maintainers may ignore tainted bug reports.
Loading your own experimental modules taints the kernel (out-of-tree flag), which is normal for development but means you should reproduce real bugs on a clean kernel.
lessons.example: A proprietary MODULE_LICENSE taints the kernel (flag P in dmesg).
lessons.pitfall: Reporting a kernel bug from a tainted kernel (your experimental module loaded) usually gets the report dismissed.

steps: Save as params.c and build it with the out-of-tree Makefile (obj-m += params.o).
Load with `sudo insmod params.ko count=3 who=kernel` and read `sudo dmesg | tail`.
Inspect `cat /sys/module/params/parameters/count` and `modinfo params.ko`.
Explain why plain gcc cannot build a loadable module.

courses.title: 3. Character devices and file_operations
courses.summary: Expose a device to user space as a /dev node: register a char device, implement file_operations, and copy data safely to user space.
courses.expected: After loading, create the node with the printed mknod command, then `cat /dev/vqchar` prints the message once and stops at EOF.

lessons.title: Devices as files
paragraphs: Unix exposes devices as special files under /dev. A character device transfers a stream of bytes (like a serial port or /dev/null); a block device transfers fixed-size blocks (like a disk). Each is identified by a major number (which driver) and a minor number (which instance).
User space opens, reads and writes the device file with ordinary file calls; the kernel routes those calls to the driver's handlers.
lessons.example: crw-rw---- 1 root root 10, 58 /dev/vqchar  -> char device, major 10 minor 58
lessons.pitfall: Confusing a character device (byte stream) with a block device (fixed blocks) leads to the wrong driver model entirely.

question.prompt: A character device transfers:

lessons.title: Registering a char device
paragraphs: register_chrdev(0, name, &fops) asks the kernel to allocate a free major number and bind it to your file_operations; it returns the major (or a negative errno). unregister_chrdev reverses it on unload.

Registration only creates the driver binding; the /dev node is created separately — by udev automatically for modern class-based drivers, or manually with mknod using the printed major number for this simple example.
lessons.example: major = register_chrdev(0, "vqchar", &fops);  // 0 = auto-assign major
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting unregister_chrdev in the exit path leaks the major number and leaves a dangling binding after rmmod.

question.prompt: register_chrdev(0, ...) with a 0 major:

lessons.title: file_operations
paragraphs: A struct file_operations maps file calls to your functions: .open, .release, .read, .write, .llseek and more. The VFS calls these when user space operates on the device file. Set .owner = THIS_MODULE so the module cannot be unloaded while the file is open.
A .read returns the number of bytes delivered, 0 at end-of-file, or a negative errno. Returning the wrong value — never signalling EOF — makes `cat` loop forever.
lessons.example: .read returns bytes read, 0 at EOF, or -errno; .owner = THIS_MODULE pins the module.
lessons.pitfall: A read handler that always returns a positive count never signals EOF, so `cat` on the device spins forever.

question.prompt: A .read handler signals end-of-file by returning:

lessons.title: Crossing the user/kernel boundary
paragraphs: A kernel driver must never dereference a user pointer directly — the address may be invalid, swapped out, or malicious. It uses copy_to_user and copy_from_user, which validate the address and may sleep on a page fault.

copy_to_user/copy_from_user return the number of bytes NOT copied (0 on full success). Helpers like simple_read_from_buffer and simple_write_to_buffer wrap this correctly, handling the offset and partial copies for you.
lessons.example: copy_to_user returns bytes NOT copied; simple_read_from_buffer wraps it with offset handling.
lessons.pitfall: Treating copy_to_user's return value as the number of bytes copied (instead of not-copied) inverts your success check.

question.prompt: copy_to_user returns the number of bytes:

steps: Save as chardev.c and build it (obj-m += chardev.o).
Load it, read the major from `sudo dmesg`, then `sudo mknod /dev/vqchar c <major> 0`.
Run `cat /dev/vqchar` and confirm it prints once and stops (EOF handled).
Remove the node (rm /dev/vqchar) and `sudo rmmod chardev`.

acceptance: cat terminates (EOF handled, no infinite loop)

courses.title: 4. Kernel memory management
courses.summary: Allocate memory in the kernel with kmalloc and vmalloc, choose GFP flags, and respect the kernel's small stack and no-float rules.
courses.expected: On load, `sudo dmesg` shows 'kmem: sum of 0..63 = 2016'; on unload the buffer is freed with no leak (confirm with kmemleak if enabled).

lessons.title: kmalloc and kfree
paragraphs: kmalloc allocates physically contiguous memory and is the kernel's everyday allocator, backed by the slab allocator. kfree releases it. kzalloc zeroes the memory; kmalloc_array guards against size overflow for N items.
Allocations are relatively small and fast but can fail, so every allocation must be checked for NULL and freed on every path, including error paths in init.
lessons.example: buf = kmalloc_array(N, sizeof(*buf), GFP_KERNEL); if (!buf) return -ENOMEM;
lessons.pitfall: Not checking kmalloc for NULL and dereferencing it crashes the kernel on memory pressure.

question.prompt: kmalloc returns memory that is:
question.explanation: kmalloc is physically contiguous; use kzalloc to zero.

lessons.title: GFP flags
paragraphs: Every allocation takes a GFP flag describing the context. GFP_KERNEL is the normal flag and may sleep to reclaim memory — it must not be used in atomic context (interrupt handlers, while holding a spinlock). GFP_ATOMIC does not sleep but can fail more easily.
Choosing the wrong flag is a classic bug: GFP_KERNEL inside a spinlock can deadlock the kernel because the allocator may try to sleep.
lessons.example: GFP_KERNEL may sleep; use GFP_ATOMIC in interrupt/spinlock context.
lessons.pitfall: Calling kmalloc(..., GFP_KERNEL) while holding a spinlock can sleep and deadlock the CPU.

question.prompt: GFP_KERNEL must NOT be used:
question.explanation: It may sleep; atomic context cannot.

lessons.title: kmalloc vs vmalloc
paragraphs: vmalloc allocates memory that is virtually contiguous but may be physically fragmented, so it can satisfy large allocations that kmalloc cannot. It is slower and the memory is not usable for DMA that needs physical contiguity.
Rule of thumb: kmalloc for small-to-medium, physically contiguous needs (and DMA); vmalloc for large buffers where physical contiguity does not matter.
lessons.example: vmalloc(size) -> large, virtually-contiguous; kmalloc -> small, physically-contiguous.
lessons.pitfall: Using vmalloc memory for a DMA transfer that requires physical contiguity corrupts data.

question.prompt: vmalloc memory is:

lessons.title: Stack, floats and leaks
paragraphs: Kernel stacks are tiny (a few KB per thread), so large local arrays or deep recursion overflow the stack and corrupt memory — allocate big buffers dynamically instead. The kernel also forbids floating point in normal code because it does not save FPU state.
There is no garbage collector: every allocation must be freed exactly once on every path. Tools like kmemleak and KASAN catch leaks and out-of-bounds access during testing.
lessons.example: Never put a large array on the kernel stack; kmalloc it instead.
lessons.pitfall: Declaring a large local buffer (e.g. char buf[8192]) on the kernel stack overflows it and corrupts memory silently.

question.prompt: Large buffers in the kernel should be:

steps: Save as kmem.c, build it, and load it; confirm `sudo dmesg` shows the sum 2016.
Change N and verify the printed sum updates accordingly.
Add an error path that returns -ENOMEM and make sure nothing is freed twice.
Explain why GFP_KERNEL is unsafe inside a spinlock.

acceptance: kfree on every path including errors

courses.title: 5. Concurrency: locks and atomics
courses.summary: Protect shared data on an SMP, preemptible kernel with mutexes, spinlocks and atomic operations, and know which to use where.
courses.expected: On load, `sudo dmesg` shows 'sync: mutex-guarded=100 atomic=100' — both counters agree because every increment was serialized.

lessons.title: Why the kernel needs locks
paragraphs: The kernel is concurrent: multiple CPUs run kernel code at once (SMP), the scheduler can preempt kernel threads, and interrupts fire at any time. Any data touched by more than one of these needs protection, or you get a race condition.

A race is a bug where the outcome depends on timing — two CPUs incrementing the same counter can lose an update. These bugs are intermittent and brutal to debug, so identify shared data and lock it from the start.
lessons.example: counter++ is read-modify-write: two CPUs can interleave and lose an increment.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming a simple counter++ is atomic on SMP is wrong; concurrent increments silently lose updates.

question.prompt: A data race happens when shared data is accessed:

lessons.title: Mutexes vs spinlocks
paragraphs: A mutex puts a waiting task to sleep until the lock is free, so it may only be used in process context where sleeping is allowed. A spinlock busy-waits (spins) without sleeping, so it is the tool for atomic context like interrupt handlers — but it must be held only briefly.
The decisive rule: you must never sleep while holding a spinlock. Since copy_to_user and most allocations can sleep, code that needs them around shared data must use a mutex, not a spinlock.
lessons.example: Mutex: can sleep (process context). Spinlock: never sleep while held (atomic context).
lessons.pitfall: Holding a spinlock across copy_to_user (which can sleep) can deadlock the CPU — use a mutex there.

question.prompt: You must never, while holding a spinlock:
question.explanation: Sleeping with a spinlock held can deadlock.

lessons.title: Atomic operations
paragraphs: For simple shared integers and bit flags, the atomic_t type and operations (atomic_inc, atomic_dec, atomic_read, atomic_cmpxchg) perform indivisible updates without a lock, which is cheaper than taking a mutex or spinlock.
Atomics are ideal for counters and reference counts. For anything more complex than a single integer operation — updating several fields together — you still need a real lock.
lessons.example: atomic_inc(&refcount);  // indivisible, no lock required
lessons.pitfall: Using several separate atomic operations to update related fields is not atomic as a group; the combination still needs a lock.

question.prompt: atomic_t is best for:

lessons.title: Deadlock and lock ordering
paragraphs: A deadlock occurs when two paths each hold one lock and wait for the other. The standard prevention is a global lock ordering: always acquire multiple locks in the same order everywhere, and release in reverse.

The kernel ships lockdep, a runtime validator that detects potential deadlocks and ordering violations during testing. Keep critical sections short and avoid calling into unknown code while holding a lock.
lessons.example: Always take lock A before lock B everywhere; lockdep flags violations.
lessons.pitfall: Acquiring locks in different orders on different paths is the classic recipe for an ABBA deadlock.

question.prompt: The standard way to prevent deadlock is:

steps: Save as sync.c, build and load it; confirm `sudo dmesg` shows both counters read 100.
Add a second function that updates a related field and protect the pair with the mutex.
Explain why replacing the mutex with a spinlock would be unsafe if the section called copy_to_user.
Describe an ABBA deadlock and how lock ordering prevents it.

courses.title: 6. Interrupts and deferred work
courses.summary: Handle hardware interrupts with top halves, and defer the real work to bottom halves such as workqueues to keep interrupt handlers short.
courses.expected: On load, `sudo dmesg` shows the 'scheduled' message immediately and then the 'deferred handler ran' message once the workqueue runs it; unload flushes it cleanly.

lessons.title: Interrupts and the top half
paragraphs: Hardware signals the CPU with an interrupt; the kernel runs the registered handler (the top half). A driver registers one with request_irq(irq, handler, flags, name, dev) and releases it with free_irq on unload.

The top half runs in interrupt context: it cannot sleep, must not call blocking functions, and should be as short as possible because it may block other interrupts. It typically acknowledges the device and schedules the heavy work for later.
lessons.example: request_irq(irq, handler, IRQF_SHARED, "mydev", dev);  // free_irq on unload
lessons.pitfall: Doing slow work or sleeping inside the top half stalls the system and can drop other interrupts.

question.prompt: An interrupt top half must:

lessons.title: Top half vs bottom half
paragraphs: To keep interrupt handlers short, the kernel splits work: the top half does the minimum (acknowledge the device, grab data) and schedules a bottom half to do the rest later with interrupts enabled. This keeps latency low.

Bottom-half mechanisms include softirqs and tasklets (which run in atomic context and cannot sleep) and workqueues (which run in process context and can sleep). You pick based on whether the deferred work needs to sleep.
lessons.example: Top half: acknowledge + schedule. Bottom half: the actual processing, later.
lessons.pitfall: Putting all the processing in the top half defeats the purpose and hurts interrupt latency across the system.

question.prompt: The bottom half exists to:

options.text: defer heavy work out of interrupt context

question.explanation: It moves slow work to later.

lessons.title: Workqueues
paragraphs: A workqueue runs deferred work in a kernel thread (process context), so its handler may sleep — allocate with GFP_KERNEL, call copy_to_user, take mutexes. You initialise a work item with INIT_WORK and queue it with schedule_work.
Before unloading, you must cancel_work_sync (or flush) the work so no handler runs against freed module memory. This is the single most important cleanup step for deferred work.
lessons.example: INIT_WORK(&w, handler); schedule_work(&w);  // cleanup: cancel_work_sync(&w)
lessons.pitfall: Unloading the module without cancel_work_sync can run the handler after the module's memory is gone — a use-after-free crash.

question.prompt: A workqueue handler runs in:

lessons.title: Choosing a deferral mechanism
paragraphs: If the deferred work must not sleep and needs low latency, a softirq/tasklet (atomic context) fits; if it may sleep, a workqueue is the choice. Tasklets are an older atomic-context mechanism and newer code often prefers threaded IRQs or workqueues.
Threaded interrupts (request_threaded_irq) let the kernel run your handler in a dedicated thread, combining a tiny hard-IRQ part with a sleepable threaded part — a clean modern pattern.
lessons.example: Needs to sleep -> workqueue; must stay atomic + low latency -> softirq/tasklet.
lessons.pitfall: Trying to sleep (kmalloc GFP_KERNEL, mutex) inside a tasklet crashes, because tasklets run in atomic context.

question.prompt: Choose a workqueue over a tasklet when the deferred work:

steps: Save as work.c, build and load it; watch `sudo dmesg` for the scheduled and deferred messages.
Add msleep(10) inside the handler to prove it runs in sleepable process context.
Remove cancel_work_sync and reason about the use-after-free risk on rmmod.
Explain why the interrupt top half must not sleep.

courses.title: 7. Exposing data with /proc and sysfs
courses.summary: Create a /proc entry with the modern proc_ops interface to publish kernel data to user space, and understand sysfs for driver attributes.
courses.expected: After loading, `cat /proc/vqinfo` prints the info line and stops at EOF; unloading removes the entry.

lessons.title: How the kernel talks to user space
paragraphs: Beyond device files, the kernel exposes information and knobs through virtual filesystems. /proc historically holds process and kernel information; sysfs (/sys) exposes a structured view of devices, drivers and their attributes. Neither is backed by disk — reads and writes call into the kernel.
These interfaces are how tools like ps, top and udev work, and how you let an administrator read a driver's state or tweak a setting with plain cat and echo.
lessons.example:
cat /proc/vqinfo and cat /sys/module//parameters/

both call into the kernel.
lessons.pitfall: Treating /proc and /sys files as real files on disk misses that every read executes kernel code live.

question.prompt: /proc and /sys files are:

options.text: virtual; reads call into the kernel

question.explanation: They are backed by kernel code.

lessons.title: Creating a /proc entry
paragraphs: proc_create(name, mode, parent, proc_ops) adds an entry under /proc (parent NULL means the /proc root). It returns a proc_dir_entry or NULL on failure, which you must check. proc_remove tears it down on unload.
The mode (e.g. 0444) sets the file permissions. Keeping /proc entries read-only unless you truly need writes avoids a whole class of input-validation bugs.
lessons.example: entry = proc_create("vqinfo", 0444, NULL, &pops); if (!entry) return -ENOMEM;
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting proc_remove in the exit path leaves a stale /proc entry whose read handler points into unloaded module memory.

question.prompt: proc_create returns NULL when:

lessons.title: proc_ops replaced file_operations
paragraphs: Before Linux 5.6, /proc entries reused struct file_operations. Since 5.6 they use a dedicated struct proc_ops with fields like .proc_read, .proc_write and .proc_lseek. Using file_operations for /proc on a modern kernel will not compile.
This is a concrete example of the kernel's unstable internal API: in-tree code is updated across the tree when an interface changes, so out-of-tree modules must track the kernel version they target.
lessons.example: static const struct proc_ops pops = { .proc_read = info_read };
lessons.pitfall: Copying an old tutorial that uses file_operations for /proc fails to build on any kernel 5.6 or newer.

question.prompt: Since Linux 5.6, /proc entries use:

lessons.title: seq_file and sysfs attributes
paragraphs: For multi-line or large /proc output, the seq_file API handles buffering and the read offset for you, avoiding the manual pagination bugs of raw read handlers. It is the recommended way to produce structured /proc output.
sysfs is preferred for driver attributes: one value per file, created as device/kobject attributes. The convention is one logical value per sysfs file, which keeps the interface clean and scriptable.
lessons.example: seq_file handles buffering/offset; sysfs convention is one value per file.
lessons.pitfall: Emitting lots of data from a raw .proc_read without seq_file leads to subtle offset and truncation bugs.

courses.title: 8. Capstone: a read/write character driver
courses.summary: Combine registration, file_operations, kernel memory and locking into a complete character driver with an in-kernel buffer you can write and read back.
courses.expected: After creating the node, `sudo sh -c 'echo hello > /dev/charbuf'` then `sudo cat /dev/charbuf` reads back 'hello' — the in-kernel buffer stored your write, serialized by the mutex.

lessons.title: A complete driver
paragraphs: This capstone is a working character driver that stores what you write and gives it back when you read. It combines registration, file_operations for both read and write, a kernel buffer for state, and a mutex to serialize concurrent access.
It is the shape of a real driver: initialise resources in init, serve file operations safely, and release everything in reverse on exit. Each earlier lesson contributes one piece.
lessons.example: init: register -> serve read/write under a lock -> exit: unregister (reverse order).
lessons.pitfall: Returning success from init while a later resource failed to set up leaves a half-built driver that crashes on first use.

question.prompt: A driver should release resources in init-failure and exit paths in:
question.explanation: Unwind in reverse to avoid leaks.

lessons.title: Holding state safely
paragraphs: The driver keeps an in-kernel buffer and a length. Because read and write can run concurrently on an SMP kernel, both take the same mutex around the buffer and length, so a reader never sees a half-written buffer.
A mutex (not a spinlock) is mandatory here because simple_read_from_buffer and simple_write_to_buffer call copy_to_user/copy_from_user, which can sleep on a page fault.
lessons.example: Both read and write take buf_lock; a mutex is required because copy_*_user can sleep.
lessons.pitfall: Guarding the buffer with a spinlock would be a bug, since the copy to/from user inside the critical section can sleep.

lessons.title: Read and write with offsets
paragraphs: cb_write uses simple_write_to_buffer to copy user data into the kernel buffer at the current offset and advance it; the driver records data_len so a later read returns exactly what was written. cb_read uses simple_read_from_buffer to return that data and signal EOF.
These helpers correctly handle the offset pointer and partial copies, which is exactly where hand-written read/write handlers usually go wrong (infinite reads, lost bytes).
lessons.example: write: simple_write_to_buffer(...); data_len = *off;  read: simple_read_from_buffer(...)
lessons.pitfall: Hand-rolling offset arithmetic in read/write instead of the simple_* helpers is the usual source of EOF and truncation bugs.

lessons.title: Testing and safety
paragraphs: Test the driver from user space: create the node, echo text into it, cat it back, and watch dmesg. Because a kernel bug can hang or crash the machine, always develop in a disposable VM and keep a serial or dmesg log to capture an oops.
Enabling KASAN and lockdep in the test kernel catches memory and locking bugs early. Signed-module and Secure Boot settings may need to allow your unsigned test module to load.
lessons.example: Develop in a throwaway VM; a kernel oops can take the whole machine down.
lessons.pitfall: Developing kernel modules on your main machine risks a hang or filesystem corruption from a single bug; use a VM.
